content: Conventional treatment for X-linked hypophosphatemia, which involves the use of oral phosphate and calcitriol, can effectively heal rickets. However, it does not consistently lead to significant increases in serum phosphate levels, nor does it reliably normalize linear growth in affected children. Some clinical trials have suggested that adding recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy to conventional treatment may enhance growth velocity, improve phosphate retention, and increase bone mineral density. However, other studies have raised concerns that this combination therapy might exacerbate the already disproportionate body stature seen in these children. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether recombinant human growth hormone therapy in children with X-linked hypophosphatemia is associated with changes in longitudinal growth, mineral metabolism, endocrine function, renal function, bone mineral density, body proportions, and any potential adverse effects. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Ovid MEDLINE. Additional handsearching of relevant journals and conference proceedings was also performed. The most recent search was completed on January 12, 2021. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared growth hormone therapy (alone or in combination with conventional treatment) to either placebo or conventional treatment alone in children with X-linked hypophosphatemia. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias in the included studies and extracted data. The certainty of the evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE criteria. Two studies, involving a total of 20 participants, were included in the review. In one crossover study, recombinant human growth hormone therapy appeared to improve the height standard deviation score (SDS or z-score). However, it remains unclear whether the therapy was responsible for a temporary increase in serum phosphate levels and the tubular maximum for phosphate reabsorption. In the second study, which was a parallel-group trial, rhGH therapy may have improved height SDS from baseline in the treatment group compared to the control group. However, after three years, no significant difference in height SDS was observed between the groups (mean difference 0.50 SDS, 95% confidence interval -0.54 to 1.54), and the certainty of this evidence was low. The treatment was generally well-tolerated in both studies, with only transient adverse effects reported in three participants. However, the certainty of this evidence was also low. There is significant uncertainty regarding whether growth hormone therapy improves serum phosphate levels or the tubular maximum for phosphate reabsorption per glomerular filtration rate (TmP/GFR), as the evidence for these outcomes was of very low certainty. Additionally, the therapy may have little to no effect on alkaline phosphatase levels, based on low-certainty evidence. In conclusion, there is insufficient high-certainty evidence to recommend the routine use of recombinant human growth hormone therapy in children with X-linked hypophosphatemia. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify its potential benefits and risks.
